prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of optical lattice clocks based on magic-wavelength trapping, which brought atomic timekeeping to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: I keep B015 (Katori, Ye) as a single-part prize. Having now read the whole round-1 exchange and my own chair summary, my scientific reasons are unchanged and my confidence in the credit is somewhat higher, because no member proposed a different or additional name. The core is one nameable invention: trapping many neutral atoms in an optical lattice at the magic wavelength, so that the light shift cancels on the clock transition while Lamb-Dicke confinement is kept. That gives the statistics of many atoms without the Doppler and recoil penalties, and it is a different physical architecture from the single-ion clocks honoured in 2012. The roles are separable: Katori for the concept and the first strontium lattice clock, Ye for taking the approach to the systematic-uncertainty frontier near 10^-18 and integrating it with many-body and comb technology. The performance is confirmed by comparisons across laboratories, species (Sr, Yb) and links, which tests uncertainty budgets and is not a repeat of one design. I do not rest this on opening support counts, and I do not treat the lack of a redefinition of the second as a scientific doubt. As the chair I put the question of how wide the committee's evidence base is: the committee should rely on the inter-laboratory comparison data as the independent confirmation, since it exists in the literature and the committee can cite it.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation remains novelty against the 2005 prize (Hall, Haensch) and the 2012 prize (Wineland, Haroche), and I accept that a member can reasonably regard lattice clocks as the next step in a line already honoured. Two names also leave out groups with real claims (SYRTE, PTB, NIST, Ludlow, Lemke, Lisdat, and single-ion work), and I cannot show that Katori and Ye are the only defensible pair; I can say only that they are the pair whose separate roles are easiest to state. On the opposite side, I should be honest that B014 opens a wholly new observational window and is the stronger candidate on that one dimension, and that my earlier first choice came from field closeness. A configuration of B015 with B014 would force one laureate to be dropped from one part under the three-person limit, and I do not think the scientific gain justifies that.

responses.point: Ranks B015 sixth because Ye's comb work partly falls under the 2005 prize, and Chair question 1 asks what wording would settle the novelty objection; Eriksson's own first choice is now B018 (Kane, Molenkamp, Hasan).
responses.response: I take your objection as the central scientific one and I have tried to meet it in the citation rather than in rhetoric. The 2005 citation concerned the optical frequency comb and laser-based precision spectroscopy as a measurement tool; the 2012 citation concerned measuring and manipulating individual quantum systems. Neither describes a many-atom neutral lattice operated at a magic wavelength. If the citation names the lattice and the achieved accuracy, and does not mention combs, a reader cannot take it as a repeat of those prizes. I would accept an even narrower wording than mine, for example 'for the optical lattice clock and its realisation at the 10^-18 level'. On B018 I agree the discovery is real and the maturity ample. My difficulty is the credit you already concede: Mele, Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang cannot be placed, and the 2016 prize touches adjacent ground. I keep B018 as my second alternative because I would find it easier to defend than B003, whose third name, Xue, is a separate experimental pillar and would make the citation a combination of two achievements.

responses.point: Prefers B014 (Halzen, Karle) as a discovery of nature in the plain sense, and states B015 should be preferred if the committee judges clean attribution to outweigh breadth of discovery; Chair question 4 asks whether the other members could accept B015 this year.
responses.response: I agree with you on the science of B014 and I said so in round 1; the point on which we differ is how much weight attribution should carry. You frame the credit as compact, Halzen as conceiver and Karle as central to construction and analysis. I do not doubt those roles, but a citation to two people for a discovery made by a collaboration of hundreds, after AMANDA and DUMAND and with Kowalski, Klein and Waxman named by others, is one the committee must defend line by line, and I am not sure it can with a diffuse-flux citation alone. Since the source evidence is still statistically modest, I would not add it to the citation either. So my position is that B015 is the safer prize this year, not that B014 is lesser science, and I keep B014 as my first alternative. If you want to move me, I would need an argument that two names can be made defensible without naming the collaboration; I do not have that argument yet.

responses.point: Supports B015 and declares a research stay in the Hall laboratory where Ye is associated; Chair question 7 asks whether this should be recorded and how it affects the weight of his support.
responses.response: I think the committee should record it as you describe it, as a background connection from a doctoral period and not a personal tie, and it should not change how the scientific case is weighed. The reasons I give for B015 are the separable roles of Katori and Ye and the cross-laboratory confirmation, and they stand without your testimony about the laboratory. I would ask only that, in the private vote, your support for B015 be understood as one of several independent assessments (Lindroth, Olsson, Johansson and Mehlig reached it for their own reasons), and not as the sole carrier of the case. I also repeat from round 1 that urgency or 'overdue' is not a criterion, and I do not rely on it.

responses.point: Ranks B015 first, regards the two-person credit as fair and notes professional familiarity with the clock community, including Devoret and Martinis as contested claimants on B039; Chair question 3 asks whether independence of the 10^-18 confirmations is established.
responses.response: On Chair question 3 I think the evidence is adequate and the committee can state it. Agreement between Sr and Yb lattice clocks at different institutions, compared through optical fibre and by other links, tests the systematic budgets of devices that do not share one design, so it is not one laboratory confirming itself. I would not ask the members for new data, but I would ask the committee to cite those comparisons in the citation's scientific background. I also agree with your caution that the clock community is small, which is why I think your declared familiarity, with no documented tie to Katori or Ye, should be recorded and does not call for recusal. My own recollection of the latest uncertainty values is from general knowledge and I have not checked it in this record.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards the magic-wavelength lattice as distinct from the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 single-system prize; I think it is but I cannot prove it, and the citation wording carries much of the argument.
Whether Katori and Ye fairly represent a field in which SYRTE, PTB, NIST and others contributed first demonstrations and performance milestones, since no member has proposed a better set of names.
Whether B014 should be preferred if the committee decides that a two-name credit for IceCube can be defended; I have not resolved this and I would not dismiss it.
Details of the history and of the current best uncertainties are from general knowledge and are not verified in this record.
statement.conflict_note: I have no recorded personal or institutional connection to Hidetoshi Katori or Jun Ye, and none is apparent from my profile for B015. For B014 my astroparticle work (PAMELA, Fermi-LAT, balloon polarimetry) is in a neighbouring field, with no documented tie to IceCube or its named candidates, and I continue to see no recusal issue, but I note possible bias from field closeness in my earlier first-place ranking. I note Kroll's declared Hall-laboratory stay and Johansson's WACQT roles, and I think the committee should record both; neither bears on my preferred configuration.
